questions.subject: Economics
questions.learningObjective: Compare wage and non-wage influences on occupational choice.
questions.prompt: A print worker turns down a higher-paying night job because the daytime post makes it possible to attend evening lessons. Which factor explains the choice?
options: A higher money wage at the daytime post
A lower national minimum wage
The compatibility of working hours with study
A rise in the supply of night workers
questions.answer: The compatibility of working hours with study
questions.explanation: Hours that permit attendance at lessons are a non-wage benefit to this worker.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.learningObjective: Analyse influences on wages and employment in a labour market.
questions.prompt: A new packaging plant starts recruiting trained machine operators in a town. Other employers continue hiring as before. In a competitive labour market, what is the likely initial effect if the market supply curve is unchanged and slopes upward?
options: Demand shifts right and the equilibrium wage rises
Supply shifts right and the equilibrium wage falls
Demand shifts left and the equilibrium wage falls
Supply shifts left and the equilibrium wage rises
questions.answer: Demand shifts right and the equilibrium wage rises
questions.explanation: The additional employer increases demand for operators at each wage, shifting the demand curve right.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.learningObjective: Analyse influences on wages and employment in a labour market.
questions.prompt: At a minimum wage above the original equilibrium, firms in a fictional market want to hire 370 workers and 450 workers offer their labour. On these figures, how many more workers offer labour than firms want to hire?
questions.explanation: The excess supply at that wage is 450 − 370 = 80.

verification.purpose: Excess supply at the minimum wage

questions.subject: Economics
questions.learningObjective: Explain how demand, supply or bargaining can cause wage differences.
questions.prompt: Two sets of workers have similar skills and productivity. One union represents nearly all workers in its occupation, and employers have few alternative recruits. The other union represents only a small share. Which reason best explains why the first union may negotiate higher pay?
options: Its workers necessarily have higher productivity
Its workers can more easily be replaced
Its members must be in the public sector
Its relative bargaining power is stronger
questions.answer: Its relative bargaining power is stronger
questions.explanation: Widespread membership and limited replacement options can strengthen a union’s bargaining position.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.learningObjective: Explain how demand, supply or bargaining can cause wage differences.
questions.prompt: Two local occupations initially have the same wage. Demand for lift technicians then rises while training limits entry in the short run. Demand and supply in the other occupation remain unchanged. What best explains a rise in the relative wage of lift technicians?
options: Their supply immediately expands faster than demand
Employers compete for workers whose supply is slow to expand
The supply of workers in both occupations must decrease
The increase in labour demand shifts the supply curve right
questions.answer: Employers compete for workers whose supply is slow to expand
questions.explanation: With limited entry, firms trying to recruit can bid wages up for technicians relative to the other occupation.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish occupational and geographical mobility and identify their influences.
questions.prompt: A laboratory assistant completes a qualification that lets her take a job as an accounting technician without moving to a different town. Which type of mobility does this illustrate?
options: Occupational mobility
Geographical mobility
International migration
Division of labour
questions.explanation: The worker changes occupation. The example describes no change of location.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish occupational and geographical mobility and identify their influences.
questions.prompt: A company cannot fill vacancies in another city because prospective workers say they cannot find affordable accommodation there. Which change would most directly reduce the barrier described?
options: Requiring additional training for the same role
Replacing interviews with written tests
Increasing the shift length
Providing temporary accommodation near the vacancies
questions.answer: Providing temporary accommodation near the vacancies
questions.explanation: Temporary accommodation addresses the housing obstacle to working in a different city.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.learningObjective: Identify benefits and costs of worker specialisation.
questions.prompt: A bakery assigns mixing, shaping and packing to separate workers. Which outcome illustrates a possible disadvantage of this division of labour?
options: Workers spend less time changing tools between operations
The production line stops when the only employee trained to shape dough is absent
Workers become more proficient at their repeated task
Training for each narrow task takes less time
questions.answer: The production line stops when the only employee trained to shape dough is absent
questions.explanation: Specialisation can make stages dependent on one another when there is no trained replacement.
